```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r packages}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(knitr)
library(modelsummary)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
pal <- c("#2a6fdb", "#d1495b", "#00a6a6", "#edae49")
```

## The question

**What predicts whether a husband is more than 5 years older than his wife?**

In Lab 7 I estimated this with OLS. Here I estimate the same models with **logit** and **probit** and ask which variables actually help predict.

## Data and sample

```{r data}
load("~/Downloads/ACS2021_couples.RData")

race_labels <- c("White" = "1", "Black" = "2",
                 "American Indian or Alaska Native" = "3",
                 "Chinese" = "4", "Japanese" = "5",
                 "Other Asian or Pacific Islander" = "6",
                 "Other race" = "7", "two races" = "8", "three races" = "9")
hisp_labels <- c("Not Hispanic" = "0", "Mexican" = "1", "Puerto Rican" = "2",
                 "Cuban" = "3", "Other" = "4")
acs2021_couples$RACE     <- fct_recode(as.factor(acs2021_couples$RACE), !!!race_labels)
acs2021_couples$h_race   <- fct_recode(as.factor(acs2021_couples$h_race), !!!race_labels)
acs2021_couples$HISPAN   <- fct_recode(as.factor(acs2021_couples$HISPAN), !!!hisp_labels)
acs2021_couples$h_hispan <- fct_recode(as.factor(acs2021_couples$h_hispan), !!!hisp_labels)

# variables my copy of the data is missing
acs2021_couples$age_diff <- acs2021_couples$AGE - acs2021_couples$h_age
educ_years <- c("N/A or no schooling" = 0, "Nursery school to grade 4" = 3,
                "Grade 5, 6, 7, or 8" = 7.5, "Grade 9" = 9, "Grade 10" = 10,
                "Grade 11" = 11, "Grade 12" = 12, "1 year of college" = 13,
                "2 years of college" = 14, "3 years of college" = 15,
                "4 years of college" = 16, "5+ years of college" = 18)
acs2021_couples$educ_numeric <- unname(educ_years[as.character(acs2021_couples$EDUC)])
acs2021_couples <- acs2021_couples %>%
  mutate(educ_hs       = as.numeric(educ_numeric == 12),
         educ_somecoll = as.numeric(educ_numeric %in% c(13, 14, 15)),
         educ_college  = as.numeric(educ_numeric == 16),
         educ_advdeg   = as.numeric(educ_numeric == 18))

# traditional couples: she is the spouse, he is the householder (h_sex 1 = Male)
trad_data <- acs2021_couples %>% filter(SEX == "Female", h_sex == 1)
trad_data$REGION <- as_factor(trad_data$REGION)

trad_data$he_more_than_5yrs_than_her <- as.numeric(trad_data$age_diff < -5)

# extra predictors
trad_data <- trad_data %>%
  mutate(her_foreign  = as.numeric(BPL >= 150),        # born outside the US
         his_foreign  = as.numeric(h_bpl >= 150),
         diff_race    = as.numeric(RACE != h_race),
         in_metro     = as.numeric(MET2013 != 0),
         food_stamps  = as.numeric(FOODSTMP == 2),
         no_insurance = as.numeric(HCOVANY == 1),
         commute_min  = as.numeric(TRANTIME),
         kids_under5  = as.numeric(NCHLT5 > 0),
         # silly variables
         mobile_home  = as.numeric(UNITSSTR == 1),
         no_heat_fuel = as.numeric(FUELHEAT == 1),
         walks_to_work = as.numeric(TRANWORK == 60),
         veteran      = as.numeric(VETSTAT == 2))

y <- trad_data$he_more_than_5yrs_than_her
```

The sample is every married couple where the wife is the spouse and the husband is the
householder: **`r format(nrow(trad_data), big.mark = ",")` couples**. In
**`r round(100 * mean(y), 1)`%** of them he is more than 5 years older.

Checking which value is 1 (it should be only the couples where `age_diff` is below −5):

```{r check}
table(y, cut(trad_data$age_diff, c(-100, -10, -5, 0, 5, 10, 100))) %>%
  as.data.frame.matrix() %>%
  `rownames<-`(c("0: not", "1: he is >5 yrs older")) %>%
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Her age minus his age, by outcome")
```

All the 1s fall in the two left columns, so a positive coefficient means *more likely that he
is more than 5 years older*. The 0s in the (−10, −5] column are couples exactly 5 years apart,
which correctly count as "not more than 5".

## Models

I estimate four logit specifications, each adding a group of variables:

| Model | Adds |
|---|---|
| 1 | Her education (dummies, vs. less than high school) and her age — the professor's model |
| 2 | Race, Hispanic origin, born abroad (each spouse), different-race couple, metro area, region |
| 3 | Model 2 plus four "silly" variables: lives in a mobile home, uses no heating fuel, walks to work, she is a veteran |
| 4 | Model 2 plus hardship and daily life: food stamps, no health insurance, commute time, kids under 5 |

```{r models, cache=TRUE}
f1 <- he_more_than_5yrs_than_her ~ educ_hs + educ_somecoll + educ_college + educ_advdeg + AGE
f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + RACE + HISPAN + her_foreign + his_foreign + diff_race + in_metro + REGION)
f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + mobile_home + no_heat_fuel + walks_to_work + veteran)
f4 <- update(f2, . ~ . + food_stamps + no_insurance + commute_min + kids_under5)

logit1 <- glm(f1, data = trad_data, family = binomial)
logit2 <- glm(f2, data = trad_data, family = binomial)
logit3 <- glm(f3, data = trad_data, family = binomial)
logit4 <- glm(f4, data = trad_data, family = binomial)
```

### Coefficients

Logit coefficients are changes in the log-odds. The table shows **odds ratios**
(exp(coefficient)): above 1 means more likely, below 1 less likely. For example, 0.5 means
half the odds. Region dummies and the smaller race and Hispanic-origin categories are
estimated but left out of the table to keep it readable.

```{r coef-table}
coef_names <- c(
  "educ_hs" = "High school", "educ_somecoll" = "Some college",
  "educ_college" = "Bachelor's", "educ_advdeg" = "Advanced degree",
  "AGE" = "Her age (per year)",
  "RACEBlack" = "Black", "RACEChinese" = "Chinese", "RACEJapanese" = "Japanese",
  "RACEOther Asian or Pacific Islander" = "Other Asian / Pacific Islander",
  "HISPANMexican" = "Mexican", "her_foreign" = "She was born abroad",
  "his_foreign" = "He was born abroad", "diff_race" = "Different-race couple",
  "in_metro" = "Lives in a metro area", "food_stamps" = "Gets food stamps",
  "no_insurance" = "No health insurance", "commute_min" = "Commute (per minute)",
  "kids_under5" = "Has kids under 5",
  "mobile_home" = "Lives in a mobile home", "no_heat_fuel" = "Uses no heating fuel",
  "walks_to_work" = "Walks to work", "veteran" = "She is a veteran")

modelsummary(list("Model 1" = logit1, "Model 2" = logit2,
                  "Model 3" = logit3, "Model 4" = logit4),
             exponentiate = TRUE, coef_map = coef_names,
             stars = TRUE, gof_map = c("nobs", "aic"), fmt = 2)
```

```{r odds-plot, fig.height=5.5}
broom::tidy(logit4, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term %in% names(coef_names), term != "AGE", term != "commute_min") %>%
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(coef_names[term], estimate)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(estimate, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), colour = pal[1]) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Odds ratio (log scale): right of 1 = more likely he is >5 yrs older",
       y = NULL, title = "What raises and lowers the odds (Model 4)")
```

**What the coefficients say:**

* **Education has large effects.** In Model 1 an advanced degree cuts the odds roughly
  in half compared with less than high school.
* **Background matters a lot.** Women born abroad have about 60% higher odds, and couples of
  different races about 30% higher. Black wives have higher odds than white wives, and
  Chinese and Japanese wives lower odds. Mexican-origin wives have lower odds than
  non-Hispanic wives.
* **The education effects shrink from Model 1 to Model 2.** Part of the education "effect" in
  Model 1 was really background, for example because less-educated women are more often
  immigrants. This is omitted variable bias.
* **Young kids:** couples with a child under 5 have much *lower* odds. This is not a cause
  (see the exogeneity section below).

## OLS vs. logit vs. probit

Using the Model 2 variables, I estimate all three and compare them. Logit and probit
coefficients are on different scales, so I convert each to an **average marginal effect**:
the average change in the *probability*, which is directly comparable to the OLS coefficient.

```{r three-methods, cache=TRUE, dependson='models'}
ols2    <- lm(f2, data = trad_data)
probit2 <- glm(f2, data = trad_data, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# average marginal effect = mean slope of the link function x coefficient
ame <- function(m) {
  xb <- predict(m, type = "link")
  dens <- if (m$family$link == "logit") dlogis(xb) else dnorm(xb)
  mean(dens) * coef(m)
}

show_terms <- c("educ_college", "educ_advdeg", "AGE", "RACEBlack", "HISPANMexican",
                "her_foreign", "diff_race")
tibble(Variable = coef_names[show_terms],
       OLS      = coef(ols2)[show_terms],
       Logit    = ame(logit2)[show_terms],
       Probit   = ame(probit2)[show_terms]) %>%
  mutate(across(OLS:Probit, ~ sprintf("%+.1f pts", 100 * .x))) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrr",
        caption = "Change in probability (percentage points), Model 2 variables")
```

The three methods tell the same story: the marginal effects are within about a percentage
point of each other.

```{r pred-compare, fig.height=4.5}
preds <- tibble(OLS    = fitted(ols2),
                Logit  = fitted(logit2),
                Probit = fitted(probit2))

set.seed(1)
preds %>% slice_sample(n = 8000) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(OLS, Probit), names_to = "method", values_to = "pred") %>%
  ggplot(aes(Logit, pred, colour = method)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal[c(2, 3)]) +
  labs(x = "Logit predicted probability", y = "Other method's prediction", colour = NULL,
       title = "Predicted probabilities, one dot per couple (random 8,000)")
```

Probit and logit predictions are almost identical (correlation
`r round(cor(preds$Logit, preds$Probit), 4)`). OLS agrees in the middle (correlation
`r round(cor(preds$Logit, preds$OLS), 3)`) but drifts apart at the ends, most of all for the couples
with the highest predicted probabilities, where the logit curve bends and the OLS straight
line can't. OLS predictions range from
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(preds$OLS))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(preds$OLS))`, so here no
prediction falls outside 0–1, but nothing in OLS prevents it.

## From probabilities to predictions

Each model gives every couple a *probability*. To compare predictions with the truth I need a
yes/no guess, so I pick a **cutoff**: predict "yes" if the probability is above it. Following
the lab, I first use the average predicted probability as the cutoff.

```{r confusion}
# share correct, share of real 1s caught, share of real 0s wrongly flagged
scores <- function(p, y, cutoff = mean(p)) {
  guess <- p > cutoff
  c(Accuracy        = mean(guess == y),
    `1s caught`     = mean(guess[y == 1]),
    `0s flagged`    = mean(guess[y == 0]),
    `Predicted yes` = mean(guess))
}

all_preds <- list("OLS (Model 2)"    = fitted(ols2),
                  "Probit (Model 2)" = fitted(probit2),
                  "Logit Model 1"    = fitted(logit1),
                  "Logit Model 2"    = fitted(logit2),
                  "Logit Model 3"    = fitted(logit3),
                  "Logit Model 4"    = fitted(logit4))

# area under the ROC curve: chance the model ranks a random 1 above a random 0
auc <- function(p, y) {
  r <- rank(p); n1 <- as.numeric(sum(y == 1)); n0 <- as.numeric(sum(y == 0))
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

map_dfr(all_preds, ~ c(scores(.x, y), AUC = auc(.x, y)), .id = "Model") %>%
  mutate(across(Accuracy:`Predicted yes`, ~ sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * .x)),
         AUC = sprintf("%.3f", AUC)) %>%
  kable(align = "lrrrrr",
        caption = "Prediction quality, cutoff = average predicted probability")
```

How to read the columns:

* **1s caught:** of the couples where he really is >5 years older, the share the model flags.
* **0s flagged:** of the couples where he isn't, the share the model wrongly flags (false alarms).
* **AUC:** the chance the model gives a higher probability to a random "yes" couple than to a
  random "no" couple. 0.5 is a coin flip, 1 is perfect.

Logit Model 4 has the best accuracy, the fewest false alarms and the highest AUC (OLS
catches slightly more real cases only because it says "yes" more often). Even so, its AUC is only
`r sprintf("%.2f", auc(fitted(logit4), y))`. OLS, logit and probit with the same variables
predict essentially equally well. **The choice of variables matters far more than the choice
of method.**

A useful benchmark: guessing "no" for everyone is right
**`r round(100 * (1 - mean(y)), 1)`%** of the time, higher than any model's accuracy at this
cutoff. Accuracy alone is a misleading score when one outcome is much more common.

### The tradeoff between false alarms and misses

```{r cutoffs, fig.height=4}
cut_grid <- seq(0.05, 0.6, by = 0.01)
p4 <- fitted(logit4)
map_dfr(cut_grid, ~ c(cutoff = .x, scores(p4, y, .x))) %>%
  select(cutoff, `Real 1s caught` = `1s caught`, `Real 0s wrongly flagged` = `0s flagged`,
         Accuracy) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cutoff) %>%
  ggplot(aes(cutoff, value, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(p4), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = mean(p4) + 0.01, y = 0.97, hjust = 0,
           label = "average-prediction cutoff", size = 3.5, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal[c(4, 1, 2)]) +
  labs(x = "Cutoff (predict 'yes' if probability is above this)", y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "Raising the cutoff: fewer false alarms, but more misses (Model 4)") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

A **low cutoff** flags almost everyone: few misses, many false alarms. A **high cutoff** flags
almost no one. Accuracy climbs toward `r round(100 * (1 - mean(y)))`% only because the model
stops saying "yes". At a cutoff of 0.5 the model predicts "no" for nearly every couple,
because only `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(p4 > 0.5))` of predicted probabilities are
above 0.5. The right cutoff depends on which mistake is worse; with no particular use in mind,
the average prediction is a reasonable middle ground.

```{r roc, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=5.5}
roc_points <- function(p, y) {
  cuts <- quantile(p, seq(0, 1, by = 0.01))
  tibble(fpr = map_dbl(cuts, ~ mean(p[y == 0] > .x)),
         tpr = map_dbl(cuts, ~ mean(p[y == 1] > .x)))
}
bind_rows(`Model 1` = roc_points(fitted(logit1), y),
          `Model 2` = roc_points(fitted(logit2), y),
          `Model 4` = roc_points(fitted(logit4), y), .id = "model") %>%
  ggplot(aes(fpr, tpr, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal[c(4, 3, 1)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Real 0s wrongly flagged", y = "Real 1s caught", colour = NULL,
       title = "ROC curves: every possible cutoff")
```

Each curve traces all possible cutoffs. Higher and further left is better; the dashed line is
random guessing. Each added group of variables lifts the curve, but none comes close to the
top-left corner.

## Where is the model most confused?

Model 4's performance within subgroups, at the average-prediction cutoff:

```{r subgroups}
sub_df <- trad_data %>%
  mutate(p = p4, guess = p > mean(p4), y = y,
         `Her education` = factor(case_when(educ_advdeg == 1 ~ "Advanced degree",
                                            educ_college == 1 ~ "Bachelor's",
                                            educ_somecoll == 1 ~ "Some college",
                                            educ_hs == 1 ~ "High school",
                                            TRUE ~ "Less than high school"),
                                  levels = c("Less than high school", "High school",
                                             "Some college", "Bachelor's", "Advanced degree")),
         `Her race` = fct_collapse(RACE,
                                   "White" = "White", "Black" = "Black",
                                   "Asian or Pacific Islander" = c("Chinese", "Japanese",
                                                                   "Other Asian or Pacific Islander"),
                                   "Two or more races" = c("two races", "three races"),
                                   other_level = "Other"),
         `Born abroad` = ifelse(her_foreign == 1, "She was born abroad", "She was born in the US"),
         `Her age` = cut(AGE, c(0, 34, 49, 64, 120),
                         labels = c("Under 35", "35-49", "50-64", "65+")))

sub_scores <- map_dfr(c("Her education", "Her race", "Born abroad", "Her age"), function(g) {
  sub_df %>%
    group_by(group = .data[[g]]) %>%
    summarise(n = n(),
              `Actual share yes` = mean(y),
              Accuracy = mean(guess == y),
              `1s caught` = mean(guess[y == 1]),
              `0s flagged` = mean(guess[y == 0])) %>%
    filter(!is.na(group)) %>%   # a few records have an implausible age of 0
    mutate(Variable = g, .before = 1)
})

sub_scores %>%
  mutate(n = format(n, big.mark = ","),
         across(`Actual share yes`:`0s flagged`, ~ sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * .x))) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Split by", "Group", "Couples", "Actual share yes",
                      "Accuracy", "1s caught", "0s flagged"),
        align = "llrrrrr", caption = "Model 4 performance by subgroup")
```

```{r subgroup-plot, fig.height=5}
sub_scores %>%
  mutate(label = fct_rev(fct_inorder(as.character(group)))) %>%
  select(Variable, label, `1s caught`, `0s flagged`) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(`1s caught`, `0s flagged`)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(value, label, colour = name)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = label), colour = "grey80", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  facet_grid(Variable ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal[c(2, 1)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL,
       title = "The model mostly sorts groups instead of individuals") +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
```

The pattern: the model mostly sorts couples *by group*. For groups with high predicted
probabilities (women born abroad, women without a high school diploma, Asian and
Pacific Islander women), it flags most of the group, so it catches most real cases but also
raises false alarms for most of the 0s. For low-probability groups (college graduates,
women 65+) it flags few couples and misses most real cases. The model is most confused for
women born abroad: it flags almost all of them, so accuracy there is only about 35%. Within a
group it has much less ability to tell couples apart, because most of the variables in the
model describe which group a couple belongs to, not the couple itself.

## Which variables earn their place?

To see how much each variable adds, I drop it from Model 4 (and the silly variables from
Model 3) one at a time and check how much worse the fit gets. A bigger increase in AIC means a
more useful variable. Factors such as race or region are dropped as a whole.

```{r drop1, fig.height=5, cache=TRUE, dependson='models'}
d4 <- drop1(logit4)
d3 <- drop1(logit3, scope = ~ mobile_home + no_heat_fuel + walks_to_work + veteran)
drop_aic <- bind_rows(
  tibble(term = rownames(d4), dAIC = d4$AIC - AIC(logit4)),
  tibble(term = rownames(d3), dAIC = d3$AIC - AIC(logit3))) %>%
  filter(term != "<none>")

nice <- c(coef_names, RACE = "Her race", HISPAN = "Hispanic origin", REGION = "Region")

drop_aic %>%
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(coalesce(nice[term], term), dAIC),
         kind = ifelse(term %in% c("mobile_home", "no_heat_fuel", "walks_to_work", "veteran"),
                       "Silly (Model 3)", "Model 4")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(dAIC, label, fill = kind)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = pal[c(1, 4)]) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(x = "How much worse AIC gets when the variable is dropped", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Most useful predictors")
```

```{r aic-table}
tibble(Model = paste("Logit Model", 1:4),
       `Coefficients` = map_int(list(logit1, logit2, logit3, logit4), ~ length(coef(.x))),
       AIC = map_dbl(list(logit1, logit2, logit3, logit4), AIC)) %>%
  mutate(`Change vs Model 2` = AIC - AIC(logit2),
         across(c(AIC, `Change vs Model 2`), ~ round(.x))) %>%
  kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","),
        caption = "Model fit (lower AIC is better)")
```

* **Most useful:** her age by far, then kids under 5, being born abroad, a college or
  advanced degree, and food stamps.
* **Little value:** metro area, commute time and no health insurance add comparatively little
  (no insurance least of all).
* **The silly variables:** together they lower AIC by only about 120 (Model 3 vs Model 2),
  compared with about 1,790 for Model 4's variables. Living in a mobile home does most of
  that: it raises the odds by about 20%, most likely as a proxy for low income. Being a
  veteran adds a little, and heating fuel and walking to work add essentially nothing.
  With 400,000 couples even tiny effects get significance stars, so stars alone don't show
  that a variable is useful.

## Are these variables exogenous?

Prediction and causation are different questions. A variable can predict well while being a
*result* of the marriage, not a cause of the age gap.

| Variable | Exogenous? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Race, Hispanic origin, born abroad | Mostly yes | Fixed before marriage |
| Her age | Yes, but tricky | It's her *current* age, so it mixes generations with which marriages last |
| Her education | Mostly | Usually finished before marriage, but some women stop or return to school because of marriage |
| Region, metro area | Partly | Couples choose where to live, possibly together after marrying |
| Kids under 5 | **No** | Having a toddler depends partly on the age gap (an older husband), not the other way round: reverse causation |
| Food stamps, no insurance | **No** | Household outcomes that depend on both spouses' jobs and ages; an older husband may be retired |
| Mobile home, no heating fuel, walks to work | **No** | Proxies for income and climate, not causes |
| She is a veteran | Mostly yes | Usually served before marrying, but there's no obvious reason it would cause an age gap |

I deliberately left out **his age**, **`age_diff`** and **his work hours**. The outcome is built
from the first two, and his hours largely reflect his age (older husbands are more often
retired). Including them would "predict" well while learning nothing.

## Conclusions

* About `r round(100 * mean(y))`% of traditional married couples have a husband more than 5
  years older. Her education, her age and immigrant background are the strongest predictors.
* **Logit, probit and OLS agree closely**: marginal effects match within about a point, and they
  predict equally well. Logit and probit are guaranteed to keep predictions between 0 and 1,
  but in this sample OLS never left that range either.
* **Adding the right variables matters more than the method.** Background variables raised
  the AUC noticeably; silly variables (mobile home, heating fuel, walking to work, veteran) added almost nothing.
* **Prediction remains weak** (AUC about `r sprintf("%.2f", auc(p4, y))`). The model sorts
  couples into higher- and lower-probability groups but can't tell couples apart within a
  group. Who marries whom depends mostly on things the census doesn't measure.
* The variables Model 4 adds that improve prediction most, young kids and food stamps, are the
  least causal. They are results of the marriage, not reasons for the age gap.
